title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problemStatement: You are given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You want to maximize profit by choosing a single day to buy and a different later day to sell. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price 1), sell on day 5 (price 6), profit = 5

approachSteps: The brute force checks every buy-sell pair, which is O(n^2) — but you never need to reconsider a buy day once a lower price has appeared, so a single pass should suffice.
Scan left to right, tracking the minimum price seen so far.
At each day, the best possible profit if you SOLD today is price_today - min_price_so_far — compute that and compare it to the best profit found so far.
Update the running minimum price whenever today's price is lower than what's been seen.
This greedy choice works because selling can only ever be profitable relative to the LOWEST price that occurred before it — no later, higher minimum could ever help.

bruteForce.approach: Check every pair of buy day i and sell day j > i, tracking the max profit.

optimalApproach: Single pass tracking the minimum price seen so far and the best profit achievable by selling at the current price.
solutionCode:
def max_profit(prices):
    min_price = float('inf')
    best_profit = 0
    for price in prices:
        min_price = min(min_price, price)
        best_profit = max(best_profit, price - min_price)
    return best_profit
timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass through the prices.
followUps: How does 'Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II' (unlimited transactions allowed) change the approach?
How would you also return WHICH two days to buy/sell on, not just the profit amount?

title: Jump Game
problemStatement: You are given an integer array nums. You start at the first index, and each element nums[i] represents the maximum jump length from that position. Return true if you can reach the last index, false otherwise.

examples.explanation: Index 3 has value 0, so you're stuck there before reaching index 4.

approachSteps: You don't need to explore every possible jump sequence (which would be exponential) — you only need to track the FARTHEST reachable index as you scan.
Track max_reach, initialized to 0 (you start able to reach at least index 0).
Scan each index i from left to right. If i is already beyond max_reach, you could never have gotten here — return false immediately.
Otherwise, update max_reach = max(max_reach, i + nums[i]) — from this reachable position, see how far you could jump.
If at any point max_reach covers the last index, you can stop early and return true; if the loop finishes without ever getting stuck, you succeeded.

bruteForce.approach: Recursive/backtracking exploration of every possible jump sequence from each reachable position.

optimalApproach: Single greedy pass tracking the farthest index reachable so far; fail fast if the current index is ever beyond that frontier.
timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass through the array.
followUps: How does 'Jump Game II' (find the MINIMUM number of jumps, not just whether it's possible) change the approach?
Why is it safe to greedily track only the farthest reach, rather than considering every intermediate reachable index separately?

title: Candy
problemStatement: There are n children standing in a line, each with a rating value given in array ratings. You must give each child at least 1 candy. Children with a higher rating than an immediate neighbor must get more candies than that neighbor. Return the minimum total candies required.

examples.explanation: Candies: [1,2,1] — the third child doesn't need more than the second since ratings are equal, not strictly greater.

approachSteps: The constraint is LOCAL and bidirectional (compare to both left and right neighbor), which makes a single left-to-right greedy pass insufficient on its own — you need to satisfy both directions.
Start every child with 1 candy (the minimum baseline).

Pass 1 (left to right): if a child's rating is higher than the child immediately to their LEFT, give them one more candy than that left neighbor. This satisfies the 'higher rating than left neighbor' constraint everywhere.

Pass 2 (right to left): if a child's rating is higher than the child immediately to their RIGHT, they need MORE candy than that right neighbor too — take the max of their current candy count and (right neighbor's candy + 1). This satisfies the 'higher than right neighbor' constraint without breaking what pass 1 already fixed.
Sum all the final candy counts for the answer.

The reason two passes (rather than one) are needed: a single pass can only correctly enforce the constraint relative to one direction at a time; the second pass corrects the other direction while preserving the first pass's guarantees (because it only ever increases counts, never decreases them).

bruteForce.approach: Iteratively re-scan and bump candy counts until no constraint is violated (a relaxation-style approach).

optimalApproach: Two greedy passes over the candy array — left-to-right enforcing the left-neighbor constraint, right-to-left enforcing the right-neighbor constraint by taking the max with the existing value.
timeComplexity: O(n) — two linear passes over the ratings array.
followUps: Why must the second pass take max(current, right+1) instead of just overwriting with right+1?
Could this be solved with O(1) extra space instead of an O(n) candies array? Sketch how.
